questions.q: Riya colours a grid of 100 squares to show the gases in air: one colour for nitrogen, one for oxygen and one for argon, carbon dioxide and other gases together. Which set of square counts is correct?
questions.a: 78 nitrogen, 21 oxygen, 1 argon, carbon dioxide and other gases
o: 78 nitrogen, 21 oxygen, 1 argon, carbon dioxide and other gases
21 nitrogen, 78 oxygen, 1 argon, carbon dioxide and other gases
78 nitrogen, 1 oxygen, 21 argon, carbon dioxide and other gases
50 nitrogen, 49 oxygen, 1 argon, carbon dioxide and other gases

questions.q: A large balloon at a school fair is filled with 200 litres of air. About how many litres of this air are oxygen?
questions.a: 42 litres

questions.q: Moving air is called wind. What does the chapter call wind that blows gently?
questions.a: A breeze

questions.q:
Match each term in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Nitrogen  2. Oxygen  3. Wind  4. Windmill farm
Column II: A. Moving air  B. The gas that makes up about 78% of air  C. An area with a large number of windmills that use the wind to generate electricity  D. The gas the body needs to perform its functions, about 21% of air

Assertion (A): We can survive without food or water for a few days, but we cannot survive without oxygen for even a few minutes.
Reason (R): Oxygen makes up about 21% of the air around the Earth.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
State whether the statement is True or False. If it is False, correct it.
Statement: Carbon dioxide makes up about 21% of the air.
questions.a: False. Oxygen makes up about 21% of the air; carbon dioxide is part of the 1% that also includes argon and other gases.
s: Says False
Corrects it: oxygen is about 21%, carbon dioxide is within the 1% with argon and other gases

questions.q: (a) Name two uses of windmills other than generating electricity. (b) What is a windmill farm?
questions.a: (a) Windmills can run flour mills and pull up water from a well. (b) A windmill farm is an area with a large number of windmills that use the energy of the wind to generate electricity.
s: (a) Names running flour mills and pulling up water from a well
(b) An area with many windmills that use wind energy to generate electricity

questions.q: A school assembly hall holds about 3,00,000 litres of air. Using the composition of air given in the chapter, find (a) the volume of nitrogen, (b) the volume of oxygen and (c) the volume of argon, carbon dioxide and other gases together in the hall.
questions.a: (a) 78% of 3,00,000 = 2,34,000 litres of nitrogen. (b) 21% of 3,00,000 = 63,000 litres of oxygen. (c) 1% of 3,00,000 = 3,000 litres of argon, carbon dioxide and other gases.
s: (a) Nitrogen: 78% of 3,00,000 = 2,34,000 litres
(b) Oxygen: 21% of 3,00,000 = 63,000 litres
(c) Other gases: 1% of 3,00,000 = 3,000 litres

questions.q: Surya runs across the courtyard holding a paper firki and it spins. When he stands still on a calm afternoon, it stops. Later he sees a windmill near Ajji's village well. (a) What makes the firki spin? (b) Why does it stop when he stands still on the calm afternoon? (c) In what way is a windmill similar to the firki? (d) Name two jobs a windmill can do for a village.
questions.a: (a) Wind, that is, moving air, makes the firki rotate; running moves the firki through the air. (b) On a calm afternoon there is hardly any moving air, and standing still he does not move the firki through the air, so nothing turns it. (c) Just as wind turns the firki, wind rotates the wings of a windmill; the working of a windmill is similar to that of a firki. (d) Any two of: pulling up water from a well, running a flour mill, generating electricity.
s: (a) Wind (moving air) makes the firki rotate
(b) No moving air reaches the firki when he stands still on a calm day
(c) Wind rotates a windmill's wings in the same way as the firki
(d) Names two of: pulling up well water, running a flour mill, generating electricity

questions.q:
A village in Kutch uses a windmill to lift water from its well into a storage tank. On a windy day the windmill lifts 400 litres of water every hour. On a calm day it lifts none. The village needs 2,000 litres of water a day for its animals and gardens. On Tuesday the wind blew for only 3 hours. The panchayat is now deciding whether to depend on the windmill alone.
(a) What turns the wings of the windmill?
(b) For how many windy hours must the windmill run to lift the 2,000 litres needed in a day?
(c) How many litres short of the daily need was the village on Tuesday?
(d) Should the village depend on the windmill alone? Give your judgement with one point for the windmill and one against depending on it alone.
questions.a: (a) Wind (moving air) rotates the wings. (b) 2,000 / 400 = 5 windy hours. (c) 3 x 400 = 1,200 litres were lifted, so the village was 2,000 - 1,200 = 800 litres short. (d) It should keep the windmill but not depend on it alone. For it: the windmill uses the energy of the wind and needs no fuel. Against: the wind does not always blow (Tuesday gave only 3 hours, and a calm day gives nothing), so the village should store extra water in the tank on windy days or keep another way of lifting water.
s: (a) Names the wind (moving air)
(b) Calculates 5 windy hours
(c) Calculates 1,200 litres lifted and 800 litres short
(d) Judges with a point for (uses wind, no fuel) and against (wind not always blowing; store water or keep a backup)

questions.q: Freshwater is found in several places on and under the Earth. Which of these is the most easily accessible for our daily use?
questions.a: Water in ponds, rivers, lakes and wells
o: Water in ponds, rivers, lakes and wells
Water locked in ice sheets near the poles
Snow lying on high mountain peaks
Water stored deep under the ground

questions.q: A leaking tap in a school washroom wastes 12 litres of water every day. If the leak is not fixed, how much water is wasted in a month of 30 days?
questions.a: 360 litres

questions.q:
Read the statements about water.
I. Water covers about two-thirds of the Earth's surface.
II. Freshwater stored in ice sheets and snow is easily accessible for daily use.
III. Stepwells store rainwater as well as water seeping in from nearby lakes, ponds and rivers.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Stepwells known as bawadis in Rajasthan and vavs in Gujarat were built for water harvesting.
Reason (R): These regions face a scarcity of water.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
State whether the statement is True or False. If it is False, correct it.
Statement: A river gets polluted only when plastic bags and wrappers are thrown into it.
questions.a: False. Throwing trash such as plastic bags pollutes water, but waste from homes and industries dumped into a river also pollutes it.
s: Says False
Adds that waste from homes and industries dumped into water also pollutes it

questions.q: A school in Chennai collects rain from its roof and stores it in an underground tank. By the end of the rainy season the tank holds 4,500 litres. (a) The school garden needs 150 litres of water a day. For how many days can the stored water alone keep the garden watered? (b) What is this method of collecting water called, and how does it help when freshwater is limited?
questions.a: (a) 4,500 / 150 = 30 days. (b) Rainwater harvesting. Rain is collected and stored for later use, so the school takes less from its limited freshwater supply.
s: (a) Calculates 4,500 / 150 = 30 days
(b) Names rainwater harvesting and says stored rain is used later instead of the limited freshwater supply

questions.q: The Khan family in Bhopal measures its water use on one day: bathing 150 litres, washing clothes 100 litres, cooking and drinking 20 litres, cleaning the house 30 litres. (a) Find the family's total water use that day. (b) Which activity uses the most water? (c) Suggest one way, from the ways given in the chapter, to reduce wastage in that activity.
questions.a: (a) 150 + 100 + 20 + 30 = 300 litres. (b) Bathing (150 litres, half of the total). (c) Turn off the tap or shower when it is not in use (for example while applying soap), and fix any leaking taps.
s: (a) Adds to 300 litres
(b) Names bathing as the largest use
(c) Gives a chapter way to cut wastage in bathing, such as turning off taps when not in use or fixing leaks

questions.q: Water covers about two-thirds of the Earth's surface, yet only a small part of it is easy for us to use. Answer in three short points: (a) Where is most of the Earth's water found? (b) Why is that water not fit for domestic, agricultural and industrial use? (c) Why is much of the freshwater also hard for us to use?
questions.a: (a) Most of the water is in oceans and seas. (b) This water is saline (salty). (c) Much freshwater is in ice sheets and snow or underground, which is difficult to access; only a very small fraction in ponds, rivers, lakes and wells is easily accessible.
s: (a) Oceans and seas
(b) It is saline or salty
(c) Freshwater in ice, snow and underground is hard to access; only a small fraction is easily accessible

questions.q: A school in Jaipur uses 6,000 litres of water on each school day. A check finds leaking taps that waste 400 litres every school day. The school can also fit rainwater harvesting on its roof, which would collect about 3,000 litres on each rainy day; July has about 20 rainy days. (a) How much water do the leaks waste in 25 school days? (b) How much rainwater could the roof collect in July? (c) For how many school days would July's rainwater meet the school's full daily need? (d) Name two more ways from the chapter, other than fixing leaks and harvesting rain, by which the school can save water. (e) The school can afford only one step this month: fixing the leaks or building the harvesting system. Which should it do first? Justify your choice using your answers.
questions.a: (a) 400 x 25 = 10,000 litres. (b) 3,000 x 20 = 60,000 litres. (c) 60,000 / 6,000 = 10 school days. (d) Turning off taps when not in use, and recycling water (for example reusing water from washing for the garden). (e) Fixing the leaks first is the better choice: it is a small repair, and it saves 400 litres on every school day of the whole year, not only in the rainy months. Rainwater harvesting collects much more in July (60,000 litres) but gives little in the dry months, so it is a good second step once the leaks are fixed.
s: (a) Calculates 10,000 litres
(b) Calculates 60,000 litres
(c) Calculates 10 school days
(d) Names two further chapter ways, such as turning off taps and recycling water
(e) Chooses a step and justifies it with the numbers (leak saving every day all year versus harvest only in rainy months)

questions.q:
On a heritage walk in Jodhpur, a Class 6 group visits an old stepwell built of stone blocks. The guide shows them that in March the water lies 8 metres below the top step. In August, after the rains, it lies only 2 metres below the top step, even though no pipe brings water to it. The walls of its trenches are lined with stone blocks that let water seep through.
(a) What is such a stepwell commonly called in Rajasthan, and in Gujarat?
(b) By how many metres did the water level rise between March and August?
(c) Name two sources of the water that fills the stepwell, and say how the stone-lined walls help.
(d) A visitor says such stepwells are of no use today. Give one reason from the chapter why harvesting water still matters.
questions.a: (a) Bawadi in Rajasthan and vav in Gujarat. (b) 8 - 2 = 6 metres. (c) Rainwater, and water seeping in from nearby lakes, ponds and rivers; the stone blocks lining the trench walls allow this water to seep into the well. (d) Freshwater sources are limited and many parts of India face a shortage of water, so storing rainwater for later use helps conserve water.
s: (a) Bawadi (Rajasthan) and vav (Gujarat)
(b) Calculates a rise of 6 metres
(c) Rainwater and seepage from nearby lakes, ponds and rivers; stone-lined walls allow seepage
(d) Freshwater is limited and there is water shortage, so harvesting conserves water

questions.q: A traffic signal on a highway keeps working although no electric wire reaches it from the town. Which device on top of it most likely supplies its electricity?
questions.a: A solar panel

questions.q: Ajji spreads fresh red chillies on a mat in the sun for several days to dry them. What does she mainly use from the Sun to dry them?
questions.a: Heat from the Sun

questions.q: Surya eats a paneer roll. The paneer was made from the milk of a cow that grazed on grass, and the roll was baked in an oven run by electricity from rooftop solar panels. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Both the energy in the paneer and the electricity for the oven trace back to the Sun.
o: Both the energy in the paneer and the electricity for the oven trace back to the Sun.
Only the oven's electricity traces back to the Sun; the paneer's energy comes from the cow.
Only the paneer's energy traces back to the Sun; the panels make electricity on their own.
Neither traces back to the Sun, because only plants use the Sun's energy.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A solar cooker first changes sunlight into electricity and then uses that electricity to cook food.
Reason (R): Solar panels capture the Sun's energy and produce electricity.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q: The Sun is the main source of energy on Earth. Name two ways in which we use the energy of the Sun directly at home, as given in the chapter.
questions.a: Any two of: drying clothes or food such as chillies and mangoes in the sun, cooking food in a solar cooker, heating water in a solar water heater.
s: Names one direct use, such as drying clothes or food in the sun
Names a second direct use, such as a solar cooker or a solar water heater

questions.q: A house in Nagpur has a solar panel and a solar water heater on its roof. (a) What does each device give the family from the Sun's energy? (b) During a week of thick monsoon clouds, the family finds that both devices work poorly. Why?
questions.a: (a) The solar panel produces electricity; the solar water heater gives hot water, using the Sun's heat directly. (b) Both work by capturing the Sun's energy, and thick clouds stop most of the sunlight from reaching them.
s: (a) Solar panel gives electricity; solar water heater heats water directly
(b) Both depend on sunlight, which the clouds block

questions.q: Rohan says, "My family cooks on a gas stove, has no solar panel and does not dry anything in the sun. So my family does not depend on the Sun for energy at all." Is Rohan right? Explain with the chain the chapter describes.
questions.a: No. His family still eats food. Plants get energy from the Sun and produce food; animals eat plants and grow; we get our food from both plants and animals. So the energy in every meal his family eats comes from the Sun, and all of us depend on the Sun as the main source of energy.
s: Says Rohan is not right
Plants use the Sun's energy to produce food, and animals eat plants
The family's food comes from plants and animals, so its energy traces back to the Sun

questions.q: For each of the four activities below, say how the Sun's energy is used: as heat directly, changed into electricity, or reaching us through food. (a) Mango slices drying on a terrace. (b) A street light glowing at night with electricity stored from a solar panel. (c) A goat getting energy by eating leaves. (d) Bath water warming in a solar water heater.
questions.a: (a) Heat directly. (b) Changed into electricity by the solar panel. (c) Through food: the leaves grew using sunlight and the goat eats them. (d) Heat directly.
s: (a) Heat used directly
(b) Changed into electricity
(c) Reaches the goat through food (leaves made using sunlight)
(d) Heat used directly

questions.q: A school in Bikaner sets up a 'Sun corner'. (a) Name the device it can use to cook dal using the Sun's energy. (b) Name the device it can use to heat water for the canteen. (c) Name the device it can use to light its corridors with electricity. (d) Its solar panels produce 6 units of electricity on each sunny day. How many units do they produce in 5 sunny days? (e) Give one reason why all three devices would work poorly on a cloudy day.
questions.a: (a) A solar cooker. (b) A solar water heater. (c) A solar panel. (d) 6 x 5 = 30 units. (e) All three use the Sun's energy, and on a cloudy day little sunlight reaches them.
s: (a) Solar cooker
(b) Solar water heater
(c) Solar panel
(d) Calculates 30 units
(e) All depend on sunlight, which clouds reduce

questions.q:
Every March the Reddy family in Anantapur dries 20 kg of fresh red chillies on its terrace. After drying, they are left with 5 kg of dried chillies. In sunny weather the drying takes 6 sunny days. This year there were 3 cloudy days in between, on which the chillies did not dry at all. A neighbour suggests buying an electric dryer that works in any weather.
(a) What does the Sun provide that dries the chillies?
(b) How many kilograms of water did the chillies lose while drying?
(c) How many days in all did the drying take this year?
(d) Should the family switch to the electric dryer? Give one point for each side and your decision.
questions.a: (a) Heat from the Sun. (b) 20 - 5 = 15 kg of water. (c) 6 sunny days + 3 cloudy days = 9 days. (d) For the dryer: it works in cloudy weather, so drying would not be delayed. For the Sun: the Sun's heat is free and the family dries chillies only once a year, in sunny March, when 3 lost days are only a short delay; the dryer would need electricity. A sensible decision is to keep drying in the sun, because the delay is small and the Sun's energy costs nothing.
s: (a) Heat from the Sun
(b) Calculates 15 kg of water lost
(c) Calculates 9 days
(d) Gives a point for each side and a justified decision

questions.q: While digging a vegetable bed, Bhoomi finds pebbles, roots and some small animals that the chapter calls natural agents for turning and loosening the soil. Which animals are these?
questions.a: Earthworms

questions.q: Which rock does the chapter say can be used as a building material, like bricks?
questions.a: Laterite

questions.q:
Read the statements.
I. Forest cover has been decreasing mainly because of human activities such as large-scale cutting of trees.
II. A lost forest can be fully restored within one or two years by planting saplings.
III. Soil from every place has the same colour, because all soil is formed from rocks.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I only

questions.q:
Match each item in Column I with its use or source in Column II.
Column I: 1. Slate  2. Laterite  3. Stone arrowheads  4. Copper
Column II: A. A metal extracted from minerals  B. A rock used for roofing  C. A rock used as a building material, like bricks  D. Tools that people have made from rocks for thousands of years

Assertion (A): Forests provide food and shelter to many wild animals, including birds and insects.
Reason (R): Every animal in a forest can survive on its own without depending on other life forms.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Name two metals that are extracted from minerals. (b) Name two things made using minerals.
questions.a: (a) Any two of aluminium, gold, copper and iron. (b) Any two of airplanes, cars, jewellery, cosmetics, and electrical and electronic equipment such as mobile phones.
s: (a) Names two of aluminium, gold, copper, iron
(b) Names two of airplanes, cars, jewellery, cosmetics, electronic equipment such as mobile phones

questions.q: Every morning a gardener in Pune sweeps up all the dry leaves that fall under the mango trees and burns them. (a) Which natural process is he stopping? (b) What will the soil under the trees miss out on?
questions.a: (a) He stops recycling in nature: fallen leaves would decay and become part of the soil. (b) The nutrients that the decaying leaves would add to the soil, which new plants use to grow.
s: (a) Stops fallen leaves from decaying in the soil (recycling in nature)
(b) The soil misses the nutrients that decaying leaves add

questions.q: A class collects three soil samples. Sample P from a farm after ploughing is dark brown and damp, with bits of leaves and earthworms. Sample Q from a building site is red and dry, with many pebbles. Sample R from a riverbank is light and sandy. (a) Give one reason why the three samples have different colours. (b) Which sample is likely to have the most nutrients from decayed material, and why? (c) Why must the students wash their hands after handling the samples?
questions.a: (a) Soils from different places contain different materials, so they can be of different colours. (b) Sample P, because it holds bits of leaves and living organisms; plant and animal matter decays and becomes part of the soil, enriching it with nutrients. (c) Soil, especially soil that has garbage in it, can carry germs that may be harmful to us.
s: (a) Different places give soils with different materials, so different colours
(b) Picks sample P and links decaying plant and animal matter to nutrients
(c) Soil may carry harmful germs

questions.q: An eco-club in Kolkata collects old mobile phones from families so that the materials inside them can be recovered. (a) What are rocks made up of? (b) Name two minerals found in a basic mobile phone. (c) About how many minerals does a basic mobile phone contain? (d) How long does the chapter say it takes for rocks to form? (e) A parent says, "There are rocks everywhere, so there is no need to recover anything from old phones." Do you agree? Justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) Rocks are made up of minerals. (b) Any two of gold, silver, copper and cobalt. (c) About a dozen minerals. (d) Thousands to millions of years. (e) No. Every phone uses about a dozen minerals, and these come from rocks, which take thousands to millions of years to form. Rocks cannot be replaced in our lifetime, so they must be conserved and used responsibly; recovering minerals from old phones means less new rock has to be dug out.
s: (a) Rocks are made up of minerals
(b) Names two of gold, silver, copper, cobalt
(c) About a dozen
(d) Thousands to millions of years
(e) Disagrees and justifies: rocks form very slowly, so minerals must be conserved and recovered

questions.q:
A hill forest near a village in the Western Ghats has about 2,000 trees. A plan to widen a road needs 500 of these trees to be cut. Many villagers object; some say they will hug the trees, as people once did to protect trees from being felled. The road company offers to plant 500 saplings on bare land 10 km away and says the loss will then be fully made up.
(a) Name the well-known Indian movement in which local women hugged trees to stop them being felled.
(b) What percentage of the forest's trees would be cut?
(c) State two ways in which the soil on the cleared slope would be affected.
(d) Is the company right that planting 500 saplings far away fully makes up the loss? Give your judgement with a reason.
questions.a: (a) The Chipko movement. (b) 500 / 2,000 = 25% of the trees. (c) Without tree roots to hold the soil, it can be washed away; and with no fallen leaves decaying on it, the soil no longer gets the nutrients they add. (d) Not fully. Planting is better than nothing, but it takes many years for new trees to grow into a forest, and the saplings are 10 km away, so they do not hold the soil on the cleared slope or give food and shelter to the animals living there. The forest should be used responsibly, cutting as few trees as possible.
s: (a) Names the Chipko movement
(b) Calculates 25%
(c) Soil washed away without roots; loses nutrients from decaying leaves
(d) Judges not fully: new forest takes many years and the saplings are elsewhere

questions.q: At a fuel station, four vehicles fill four different fuels. Which of these fuels is NOT obtained from petroleum?
questions.a: Compressed Natural Gas (CNG)

questions.q: Fifty years ago most homes in a village near Mysuru cooked on wood and dung cakes. Today most use LPG or natural gas. What reason does the chapter give for this change being better?
questions.a: Natural gas and LPG are less polluting.
o: Natural gas and LPG are less polluting.
Natural gas and LPG are renewable resources.
Natural gas and LPG are human-made, not taken from nature.
Natural gas and LPG form within a few years.

questions.q: Two auto-rickshaws in Delhi carry the same passengers on the same route: one runs on CNG and the other on diesel. Which statement fits the chapter?
questions.a: CNG is a cleaner fuel than diesel, though both are fossil fuels.
o: CNG is a cleaner fuel than diesel, though both are fossil fuels.
CNG is not a fossil fuel, so its supply will never run out.
Diesel is the cleaner fuel because it comes from petroleum.
CNG is made from coal, so it pollutes more than diesel does.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): We will soon run out of fossil fuels if we continue to use them the way we do now.
Reason (R): Fossil fuels are found in limited quantities and take millions of years to form.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
State whether the statement is True or False, and give a reason.
Statement: Petrol, diesel and kerosene are all obtained from the same fossil fuel.
questions.a: True. Petrol, diesel and kerosene are all obtained from petroleum, which is a fossil fuel.
s: Says True
Reason: all three are obtained from petroleum, a fossil fuel

questions.q: A city bus can carry 50 office workers, while a car carries at most 4 people. (a) At least how many cars would be needed to carry the same 50 workers? (b) Using the chapter, give one reason why the workers taking the bus helps the city.
questions.a: (a) 50 / 4 = 12.5, so at least 13 cars are needed. (b) Using public transport means far fewer vehicles burn fossil fuels, so fossil fuels are conserved and less smoke and carbon dioxide pollute the air.
s: (a) Works out 50 / 4 = 12.5 and rounds up to 13 cars
(b) Public transport conserves fossil fuels and reduces smoke and carbon dioxide

questions.q: Answer briefly about fossil fuels. (a) Name the three fossil fuels. (b) From the remains of which living things were they formed? (c) How long does it take for these fuels to form?
questions.a: (a) Petroleum, natural gas and coal. (b) From the remains of microorganisms and plants that got buried deep inside the earth. (c) Millions of years.
s: (a) Petroleum, natural gas and coal
(b) Remains of microorganisms and plants buried deep in the earth
(c) Millions of years

questions.q: A Class 6 group in Indore surveys 70 vehicles in its neighbourhood: 40 scooters on petrol; 15 cars, of which 9 run on petrol and 6 on diesel; 10 auto-rickshaws on CNG; and 5 trucks on diesel. (a) Which fuel is used by the largest number of vehicles, and by how many? (b) How many of the 70 vehicles use a fuel obtained from petroleum? (c) Which vehicles use the fuel the chapter calls cleaner than petrol or diesel, and what fraction of the 70 vehicles are they?
questions.a: (a) Petrol: 40 scooters + 9 cars = 49 vehicles. (b) Petrol and diesel come from petroleum: 49 + 6 + 5 = 60 vehicles. (c) The 10 auto-rickshaws on CNG, which is 10/70 = 1/7 of the vehicles.
s: (a) Petrol, used by 49 vehicles
(b) Counts petrol and diesel users: 60 vehicles
(c) The CNG auto-rickshaws, 10/70 = 1/7

questions.q: Ajji cooked on wood and dung cakes when she was young; today her daughter in the city cooks on natural gas from a pipeline. Ajji's grandson says, "Wood comes from forests, which are renewable, so we should all go back to cooking on wood." (a) Why did natural gas replace wood and dung cakes in many homes? (b) Is natural gas renewable? Give the reason. (c) Why is a forest not a quick or endless source of wood? (d) Do you agree with the grandson? Give your judgement.
questions.a: (a) Natural gas is less polluting than wood and dung cakes. (b) No. It is a fossil fuel found in limited quantity that takes millions of years to form, so it is non-renewable. (c) Forests are renewable, but it takes many years to grow a new forest, and forest cover is already decreasing because of large-scale cutting of trees. (d) Not fully. Going back to wood would cause more pollution and cut more trees faster than forests can regrow. The family should keep using natural gas but use it carefully because it is limited, and where possible use the Sun's energy, for example a solar cooker on sunny days.
s: (a) Natural gas is less polluting
(b) Non-renewable: limited, takes millions of years to form
(c) New forests take many years to grow; forest cover is decreasing
(d) Judges the claim, weighing pollution and forest loss against the limited supply of natural gas

questions.q:
The Sharma family in Lucknow drives its petrol car about 600 km every month. The car runs about 15 km on one litre of petrol. Many of their trips are short ones, to the market 1 km away or to a school 2 km away. Their city also has a good bus service. The family wants to cut its petrol use.
(a) From which fossil fuel is petrol obtained?
(b) How many litres of petrol does the car use in a month?
(c) Name the two things produced when petrol is burnt that pollute the air.
(d) Suggest two ways from the chapter for the family to use less petrol on its short trips.
questions.a: (a) Petroleum. (b) 600 / 15 = 40 litres a month. (c) Smoke and carbon dioxide gas. (d) Walking or cycling to nearby places such as the market, and using public transport such as the bus.
s: (a) Petroleum
(b) Calculates 40 litres
(c) Smoke and carbon dioxide
(d) Walking or cycling, and using public transport

questions.q: Which pair has one natural resource and one human-made resource?
questions.a: Coal and an electric bulb

questions.q: Ajji lets the children collect only the nellikai (gooseberries) that have fallen on the ground, and never pluck them from the tree. How does this help the gooseberry trees stay a renewable resource?
questions.a: Fruits left for birds and animals spread seeds in their droppings, and new trees grow from them.
o: Fruits left for birds and animals spread seeds in their droppings, and new trees grow from them.
Fallen fruits sink into the soil and slowly turn into a fossil fuel such as coal over the years.
Fallen fruits are the only ripe fruits, so plucking would waste the unripe ones.
Plucking fruits by hand would turn the tree into a human-made resource instead of a natural one.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
I. Water is a renewable resource.
II. In this chapter, soil and rocks are grouped as non-renewable resources.
III. Natural gas is non-renewable because once it is used it gets exhausted and is not replenished within a reasonable period.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I, II and III

questions.q:
Match each item in Column I with its correct group in Column II.
Column I: 1. Forest  2. Coal  3. Solar panel  4. Marble
Column II: A. Human-made resource  B. Natural, non-renewable: a rock  C. Natural, renewable  D. Natural, non-renewable: mainly used to produce electricity
What are renewable resources? Give one example.
questions.a: Renewable resources are resources that get renewed, replenished or restored by natural processes within a reasonable period of time. Example: air, water or forests.
s: Defines renewable resources as those renewed or replenished by nature within a reasonable period
Gives one example such as air, water or forests

questions.q: A carpenter in Saharanpur makes a wooden table. (a) Is the table a natural resource or a human-made resource? Give a reason. (b) The wood comes from a forest. Is a forest renewable or non-renewable, and what must be kept in mind while using it?
questions.a: (a) Human-made, because it is made by people using a natural resource (wood). (b) Renewable, since nature renews forests; but a new forest takes many years to grow, so trees must be used responsibly, giving the forest time to regenerate.
s: (a) Human-made, made by people from a natural resource
(b) Renewable, but it takes many years to regrow, so use it responsibly

questions.q: Look at this list: air, coal, water, minerals, forests, natural gas. (a) Which of them are renewable resources? (b) Which are non-renewable resources? (c) Give one reason why the non-renewable group is called so.
questions.a: (a) Air, water and forests. (b) Coal, minerals and natural gas. (c) They are found in limited quantities and are not replenished within a reasonable period of time; once used, they get exhausted.
s: (a) Air, water and forests are renewable
(b) Coal, minerals and natural gas are non-renewable
(c) Limited and not replenished within a reasonable period

questions.q: For each daily activity, name the main natural resource it uses and say whether that resource is renewable or non-renewable. (a) Making clay toys. (b) Collecting firewood for a stove. (c) Cooking on a stove fed by natural gas from a pipeline.
questions.a: (a) Soil (clay), which is non-renewable. (b) Forest (wood), which is renewable. (c) Natural gas, which is non-renewable.
s: (a) Soil, non-renewable
(b) Forest wood, renewable
(c) Natural gas, non-renewable

questions.q: Compare renewable and non-renewable resources under these four headings: (a) what happens to them after use, (b) the time nature takes to replace them, (c) two examples of each, and (d) how carefully we should use each, with a reason.
questions.a: (a) Renewable resources get renewed, replenished or restored by nature; non-renewable resources get exhausted once used. (b) Renewable ones are replaced within a reasonable period of time; non-renewable ones take a very long time, for example millions of years for fossil fuels. (c) Renewable: air, water, forests; non-renewable: coal, petroleum, natural gas, minerals, soil, rocks. (d) Both must be used judiciously: non-renewable resources because they are limited and will run out, and renewable resources because nature needs time to renew them (for example a new forest takes many years to grow).
s: (a) Renewed by nature versus exhausted once used
(b) Reasonable period versus a very long time such as millions of years
(c) Two correct examples of each
(d) Both used judiciously, with a reason for each

questions.q: A school canteen in Hyderabad checks what it uses in one day: water from a borewell, natural gas for the stove, wooden benches, steel plates, rice and vegetables, and sunlight to dry washed plates. (a) Name two natural resources the canteen uses directly. (b) Name two human-made resources it uses. (c) Which natural resource in the list is non-renewable and burnt every day? (d) Suggest one way to cut the canteen's use of that resource. (e) The canteen head says, "Water is renewable, so we need not worry how much we use." Do you agree? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Any two of water, natural gas, sunlight, and food from plants (rice and vegetables). (b) Wooden benches and steel plates. (c) Natural gas. (d) Use the Sun's energy, for example a solar cooker or a solar water heater, for part of the cooking or heating (or another sensible saving, such as turning the flame off when it is not needed). (e) No. Water is renewable, but usable freshwater is limited and many places face water shortage, so even renewable resources must be used judiciously, without wasting them.
s: (a) Names two natural resources such as water and sunlight
(b) Names wooden benches and steel plates
(c) Natural gas
Suggests a sensible way, such as using solar energy (solar cooker or water heater)
(e) Disagrees: freshwater is limited, so renewable resources must also be used judiciously
